outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Punctuation.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: The use of marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications to indicate structure and meaning in writing.
A punctuation mark, space, or non-segmental modification such as italics or capitals.
Occupying a position in the linear sequence of writing, as marks and spaces do.
A modification such as italics, bold face or capitalisation that does not occupy a separate position.
A written symbol such as a comma, full stop or question mark.
A graphical shape used to realise one or more punctuation indicators.
A full stop, question mark or exclamation mark marking the end of an orthographic sentence.
A comma, semicolon or colon marking boundaries within or between clauses.
A comma pair enclosing a supplement or parenthetical element.
A pair of round or square brackets enclosing material.
A punctuation indicator used for interruption, supplement or range.
A paired indicator enclosing quoted or highlighted material.
The use of upper-case letters for sentence beginnings, proper names or emphasis.
A unit of writing beginning with a capital and ending with a primary terminal.
A minimal unit of writing flanked by spaces or punctuation.
A word-internal mark joining parts of a compound or a line break.
A mark used in some styles to join coordinated names or relationships.
A word-internal mark used for omission or the genitive.
Three dots marking omission or a trailing off.
A full stop marking an abbreviation, as in Col. Blimp.
A mark used for alternatives, fractions, dates or line breaks.
A style using relatively few optional marks, especially commas.
A style using more optional marks, especially commas.
Coordination without an overt coordinator.
A detached element set off from the clause, often by commas, dashes or parentheses.
An expression naming the person addressed, often set off by commas.
An expression such as however that links a clause to surrounding discourse.

options.feedback: Spaces are segmental punctuation indicators.
Meaning is not a punctuation indicator.
Syllables are phonological, not punctuation.

opening.prompt: Which mark is a primary terminal?

options.feedback: It marks the end of an orthographic sentence.
A comma is a secondary boundary mark.
A hyphen is word-internal.

options.text: A capital at the beginning and a primary terminal at the end
options.feedback: It is a unit of writing.

options.text: A clause with a subject and predicate
options.feedback: That is a syntactic definition.
A paragraph can contain several sentences.

options.text: They enclose a supplement or parenthetical element.
options.feedback: They mark both boundaries.
That is an abbreviation full stop.
A question mark does that.

opening.prompt: Why are apostrophe and single quotation mark distinct indicators?

options.text: They have different functions even when realised by the same character.
options.feedback: The apostrophe marks omission or genitive; the quotation mark marks quotation.
They can share a character.
Both are segmental.

closing.prompt: Why are spaces part of punctuation?

options.text: They are segmental units that separate words in writing.
options.feedback: They occupy positions in the linear sequence.
Spaces are segmental.
They mark word boundaries too.

closing.prompt: What is the difference between light and heavy punctuation?

options.text: Light uses fewer optional marks; heavy uses more.
options.feedback: The difference concerns optional commas and similar marks.

options.text: Light is grammatical; heavy is ungrammatical.
options.feedback: Both are conventional styles.
Full stops are required in both.

closing.prompt: What do the commas do in My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida?

options.text: They delimit a supplementary relative clause.
options.feedback: The relative adds information rather than restricting.
There is no coordination.
No abbreviation is involved.

closing.prompt: What is the difference between parentheses and dashes in supplements?

options.text: Parentheses tend to background; dashes tend to foreground or interrupt.
options.feedback: The effect is stylistic and rhetorical.

options.text: Parentheses are grammatical; dashes are ungrammatical.
options.feedback: Both are grammatical.
That is a different function.

options.text: It is a writing system using marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications.
options.feedback: It is not a direct transcription of speech.

options.text: It is exactly the same as prosody.
options.feedback: Punctuation and prosody are related but distinct.
Light and heavy styles show optional variation.
